Chapter 4: Tradition, Culture, and the Inherited Stories We Live By
Picture this: a small town, a family gathered around the table for a holiday meal. The dishes are familiar—each one made just the way grandma used to do it, recipes handed down through the years. As everyone digs in, stories start to flow. Some spark laughter, others bring a quiet pause, but all of them are stitched right into the fabric of family life.
There’s something deeply comforting about these rituals, isn’t there? They give us a sense of belonging—a feeling that we’re part of something bigger than ourselves.
But here’s something to think about: these traditions carry more than warm memories. They actually shape how we see the world, what we value, and the choices we make. Most of us inherit our beliefs from the culture around us, rarely stopping to ask—where do these beliefs actually come from? And do they still make sense for who we are now?
Culture is powerful. It’s like a lens that colors everything we see, offering answers to some of life’s biggest questions. But it can also act as a set of invisible rules, quietly steering our behavior. We end up following them, not because we’ve thought them through, but simply because, well, that’s just how things are done.
Let me share a story. Imagine a young person moving to a new city, hoping for a fresh start. At first, everything feels strange—the food, the way people talk, the customs on the street. But over time, they start to adapt, picking up new habits and ways of thinking. Still, every now and then, they catch themselves slipping back into old patterns—habits shaped by the culture they grew up in. It’s a reminder that culture isn’t just something “out there.” It lives inside us, shaping our choices in ways we don’t always notice.
Traditions can be a real source of strength. They connect us to our past and to each other. But sometimes, tradition can turn into a kind of superstition—something that holds us back from making changes we need. Picture a community facing a new challenge. Some people cling to the old ways, hoping what worked before will work again. Others are willing to experiment, to try something new. That push and pull between tradition and innovation? It’s just part of being human.
Most folks don’t realize just how much their beliefs are shaped by the stories they inherit. Myths, legends, even family tales—all of these shape our sense of who we are. And it’s not just old stories—scientific ideas, too, are influenced by culture. What’s considered “rational” or “true” often depends on the values of the society where those ideas are born.
Here’s another example. Picture a scientist raised in a culture that values harmony over conflict. When they discover something controversial, they hesitate to share it, afraid of rocking the boat. It’s only with the encouragement of colleagues from different backgrounds that they finally speak up. That experience reveals just how deeply culture shapes not only what we believe—but how we act.
The stories we inherit aren’t always obvious. They’re tucked into our language, our customs, even our institutions. They quietly set our expectations—what we think is possible, what we should want, and what’s off-limits. Most of us follow these stories without even realizing it. It’s only when we run into something new—something that doesn’t fit—that we start to notice them.
So, here’s the real challenge: becoming aware of these inherited stories, looking at them with fresh eyes, and deciding which ones still serve us. It’s not about rejecting tradition just for the sake of it. It’s about making conscious choices. Because when we understand the role culture plays in shaping our beliefs, we can start to take charge of our own lives—instead of just following the script that’s been handed to us.
